post-body:
Quick answer · no carpet to sell you

The best carpet for stairs is a dense, low-pile nylon with a tight twist — a short frieze or firm textured cut pile at 35–50 oz face weight — over a firm 8 lb pad no thicker than 7/16". Expect roughly $14–$36 per step installed at 2026 market rates, and avoid big-loop berber if anyone in the house has claws. Full disclosure: we're OC Flooring, a hard-surface company — we don't install carpet, but we build and remodel stairs every week, so we see how every stair covering ages.

Kenmore & King County 2026 market prices (425) 595-1079

Stairs are the hardest test a carpet ever faces. Every trip lands full body weight on the same few inches of each step, the carpet bends over a hard edge, and you can't hide the wear under a rug. We're OC Flooring — a hardwood, vinyl plank, and laminate company serving King and Snohomish County since 2013. We don't sell carpet, which puts us in a useful position here: we remodel staircases for a living, we tear worn carpet off them constantly, and we have no sample book to steer you toward. Here's what survives on stairs, what it costs at 2026 market rates, and the alternative that's quietly become the default in Kenmore remodels.

Why Stairs Chew Through Carpet Faster Than Any Room

$14–$36

per step installed — the typical 2026 market range for decent carpet on a straight staircase. Stairs price per step, not per square foot; the labor is in the folding and stapling.

steps in a typical staircase. Per-step pricing scales fast, and shaped steps — winders, pies, landings — cost more than straight ones.

2×

how much faster stair carpet visibly wears versus the same carpet in a bedroom. The nosing — the front edge of each tread — takes nearly all of it.

Three things make stairs brutal on carpet. Concentrated traffic: a hallway spreads footsteps across its width; a staircase funnels every one onto the same narrow strip. The nosing: carpet stretched over each tread's front edge gets ground between shoe and hard edge on every step — stair carpet always fails there first, fuzzing, then flattening, then bare backing. No rotation: you can turn a rug to spread wear; a staircase offers no mercy. So buy one grade tougher than the connected hallway, and treat "soft luxury" samples with suspicion — softness and stair survival pull in opposite directions.

The Winning Spec: Dense, Low, and Tightly Twisted

On stairs, construction beats color every time. You want a cut pile under about 3/4" tall, with high twist and high density — a short frieze or firm textured plush. Twist is what lets fibers spring back after being crushed against the nosing all day. Do the finger test on any sample: press into the pile and try to reach the backing — the harder that is, the better it will hold its shape bent over a step. Here's the showroom, stair-rated:

Carpet optionOn stairsVerdict
Frieze / high-twist nylonBest crush recovery at the nosing; hides wearFirst choice
Dense textured plushSofter look, very good recovery if density is highSolid choice
Small-loop nylon berberWears well but loops can snag and runPet-free homes only
Big-loop olefin berberSnags, zippers, crushes flat at the nosingAvoid
Deep saxony / shagMats fast; thick pile makes footing vagueAvoid
WoolBeautiful, resilient, premium price, careful cleaningA splurge that works

On fiber: nylon first. It's the most resilient carpet fiber made, and stairs are the one place we'd never substitute away from it. Triexta is an acceptable second, with better stain resistance for kids. Polyester belongs in bedrooms — it mats at the nosing years early. Our carpet brand review helps decode sample books, but on stairs the fiber and density lines matter far more than the brand on the spine.

The Loop-Pile Warning Every Dog Owner Should Read

Loop carpet has one failure mode stairs make worse: snagging. A dog's claw — or a vacuum edge — catches one loop, and because loops run in continuous rows, one pull can zipper a run across the step like a snagged sweater. On flat floors that's an annoyance; on a stair nosing, where claws dig in on every descent, it's a matter of months. If your household includes animals, choose a cut pile, full stop — and see our guide to flooring for kids and pets for how the rest of the house shakes out.

Pad Choice: Firm and Thin Beats Soft and Thick

This is the most common stair mistake we see, because it feels backwards: the plush pad that makes a bedroom feel luxurious will ruin a staircase. Thick, soft pad lets carpet flex and shift over the nosing with every footfall — accelerating backing fatigue and making steps feel mushy underfoot, a real problem for anyone unsteady. The spec that works: 8 lb density rebond, 3/8" to 7/16", and no thicker. On stairs, durability comes from density, not cushion. Upgrading a bargain 6 lb pad costs a few dollars a step and is the best money on the whole job.

Runner vs. Full Wrap: The Two Ways to Carpet a Staircase

A full wrap covers every inch of tread and riser, two ways: waterfall, where carpet flows over the nosing and down the riser in one piece (faster, cheaper, rounded look), or cap-and-band — Hollywood style — tucked tight under each nosing for a tailored profile (more labor, better looking). A runner covers the center walking path in a standard 27", 32", or 36" width, leaving finished wood at the edges.

The runner is the option to think hardest about, for one practical reason: it's replaceable. When the walking path wears out — on stairs, it will — you swap the runner instead of re-carpeting the staircase. It also splits every trade-off: wood looks and resale appeal at the edges, traction and quiet down the middle.

The Honest Alternative: Hardwood Stairs with a Runner

Here's where we do have skin in the game, so we'll flag it plainly. A large share of our stair remodeling work in Kenmore is exactly this: replace worn carpeted stairs with solid hardwood treads and clean risers — matched to the hardwood flooring nearby — then let the homeowner add a runner from any carpet shop. You get carpet's safety where feet land, wood's durability and resale appeal everywhere else, and a wear layer you renew for the cost of a rug. Two honest notes: some older staircases hide solid treads that can be refinished rather than replaced — we check at the estimate — and our stair installation overview shows what a remodel involves. Bare polished treads plus socks are slippery, so if you go wood, the runner is part of the plan, not optional decor.

Safety: Kids, Grandparents, and the Dog

Stair falls are the household accident that matters most. Carpet helps two ways — traction and softer landings — but only if you spec it right:

Do this
  • Low, dense pile — firm footing, clear step edge
  • Firm thin pad, stretched drum-tight
  • Runners secured with gripper rods or staples, never loose treads
  • Good lighting and a solid handrail — cheap and proven
Not this
  • Thick plush or shag — it blurs the step edge
  • Soft 6 lb pad that shifts underfoot
  • Big-loop berber in homes with pets or heels
  • Bare polished treads if anyone unsteady uses the stairs

The catch is the replacement cycle — stair carpet in a busy household looks tired in 5–8 years, so you buy the job repeatedly. That recurring bill is what makes the wood-plus-runner math interesting over a decade, the same logic we walk through in what carpet should cost in the Seattle market.

Kenmore Stairs, Specifically

Kenmore's housing stock makes this topic unusually relevant. The neighborhoods that filled in from the 1950s through the 1970s — Moorlands, Inglewood, the streets above the Burke-Gilman — are full of split-entries and tri-levels, and a split-entry puts its staircase two feet from the front door. It's the first thing every guest sees, so worn stair carpet drags down the whole entry — and this one staircase punches far above its square footage at resale.

Kenmore life is also hard on stairs in a specific way: this is a trail-and-lake town. Wet shoes from the Burke-Gilman, sandy feet from Log Boom Park, muddy paws from Saint Edward's trails — much of it headed straight up from the front door. That argues for nylon over anything absorbent, flecked colors over pale ones, and honestly for wood treads with a washable runner in the busiest households. Newer three-story townhomes near downtown have the opposite problem — the staircase is the home's hallway — so spec it like a corridor: dense, low, dark, nylon.

Stair Carpet Questions, Answered Honestly

What is the best carpet for high-traffic stairs?
A dense, low-pile nylon with a high twist — a short frieze or firm textured cut pile at 35–50 oz face weight over a firm 8 lb pad. That spec survives the nosing wear that kills stair carpet. Avoid big-loop berber and deep plush.
How much does it cost to carpet stairs in 2026?
Typical market rates run $14–$36 per step installed — budget waterfall jobs from about $10, premium cap-and-band up to $45, tear-out-and-replace $22–$65+. Market figures, not our quotes — we don't sell carpet.
Is berber carpet OK on stairs if we have a dog?
We'd avoid it. Claws catch loops, one pulled loop can zipper a run across the step, and stairs are where dogs dig in hardest. If you love the flecked look, choose a cut pile with berber styling instead.
What pad should go under stair carpet?
Firm and thin: 8 lb density rebond at 3/8 to 7/16 inch. Thick soft pad lets carpet shift over the nosing, wearing it out early and making steps feel unstable underfoot.
Are carpeted stairs safer than wood stairs?
Generally yes — carpet adds traction and softens falls, which matters for kids, older adults, and dogs. Low dense pile is safest; thick plush blurs the step edge. Wood stairs are fine with a secured runner, but bare polished treads plus socks is the slipperiest combination in the house.
How long does carpet last on stairs?
Roughly half as long as the same carpet in a bedroom — call it 5–8 years for mid-grade in a busy household. Wear concentrates on the nosing, which is why a replaceable runner over wood treads is such a practical setup.
Does OC Flooring install carpet?
No — we're a hard-surface company: hardwood installation and refinishing, vinyl plank, and laminate across King and Snohomish County. We do build and remodel stairs, and many clients pair our hardwood treads with a runner from a carpet shop.
